rows.source: Home Office and GOV.UK workplace fire-safety guidance
rows.verified: A responsible person can be an employer, owner, landlord, occupier or another person controlling non-domestic premises.

rows.source: Home Office and GOV.UK workplace fire-safety guidance
rows.verified: Where several responsible persons share premises, they must coordinate their fire-safety arrangements.

rows.source: Home Office and GOV.UK workplace fire-safety guidance
rows.verified: The responsible person must carry out and regularly review a fire-risk assessment.

rows.source: Home Office and GOV.UK workplace fire-safety guidance
rows.verified: The assessment must identify fire hazards and people who may be at risk.

rows.source: Home Office and GOV.UK workplace fire-safety guidance
rows.verified: Risks should be removed or reduced and the significant findings recorded.

rows.source: Home Office and GOV.UK workplace fire-safety guidance
rows.verified: An emergency plan, staff information, instruction and training form part of the required controls.

rows.source: Home Office and GOV.UK workplace fire-safety guidance
rows.verified: Escape arrangements should include clear routes, adequate exits, emergency lighting where needed and a safe assembly point.

rows.source: Home Office and GOV.UK workplace fire-safety guidance
rows.verified: Fire arrangements must take account of people who need additional assistance to evacuate.

rows.source: Home Office and GOV.UK workplace fire-safety guidance
rows.verified: Fire-safety duties depend on the premises use, occupancy, building layout, responsible-person arrangements, hazards, vulnerable people and current control condition.

rows.source: Home Office and GOV.UK workplace fire-safety guidance
rows.verified: General fire-safety guidance does not prove that a specific parcel has compliant systems or quantify its current fire probability.

rows.source: HSE electrical safety at work guidance
rows.verified: Electrical hazards include shock, burns, arcing, fire, explosion and ignition of flammable vapours or dusts.

rows.source: HSE electrical safety at work guidance
rows.verified: Electrical equipment that appears faulty should be removed from use and checked by a competent person.

rows.source: HSE electrical safety at work guidance
rows.verified: Inspection and testing frequency should reflect the equipment, environment and previous defect history.

rows.source: HSE electrical safety at work guidance
rows.verified: Electrical installations should be inspected and tested often enough to prevent deterioration becoming dangerous.

rows.source: HSE electrical safety at work guidance
rows.verified: Specialised electrical equipment should be inspected by a person competent for that type of equipment.

rows.source: HSE electrical safety at work guidance
rows.verified: Before work starts, energy sources should be securely isolated and exposed conductors proved dead with suitable test equipment.

rows.source: HSE electrical safety at work guidance
rows.verified: Residual current devices can reduce some shock risks but do not protect against every type of electrical injury.

rows.source: HSE electrical safety at work guidance
rows.verified: Equipment used in harsh, wet or damage-prone environments generally needs more demanding checks and controls.

rows.source: HSE electrical safety at work guidance
rows.verified: Electrical risk depends on voltage, current path, environment, equipment condition, earthing, protection devices, isolation and the exact task.

rows.source: HSE electrical safety at work guidance
rows.verified: Area-level electrical guidance does not establish the condition of a particular installation or an exact parcel-level shock, fire or explosion probability.
